bodyHtml:
How to select CMLs and TMLs on a piping circuit: a practical guide

Short answer: select condition monitoring locations (CMLs) circuit by circuit, starting from the damage mechanisms you expect, not from the geometry. Put them where those mechanisms act first: fittings, flow disturbances, dead legs, low points, injection and mix points, soil-to-air interfaces, spec breaks and insulated sections with CUI potential. Add more where the consequence or the corrosion rate is higher, and fewer on long, low-risk straight runs. Then mark each one so the same spot is measured every time. API 570 and API RP 574 set out the criteria. The authorized piping inspector applies them.

The sections above describe how we run piping circuit inspection. This guide goes one level deeper into selection itself. It covers what the terms mean, including the "CML port" and "thickness monitoring location" phrasing people search for. It then covers a step-by-step selection workflow, placement by component, how to choose the measurement technique at each CML, and how to add, move or retire CMLs without breaking the history. Code points are paraphrased from API 570 (current edition: 5th, February 2024, with Addendum 1 in 2025) and API RP 574 (reissued as a 5th edition alongside it). Where we refer to clause content, it was read from the 4th edition of API 570. Check your licensed current copy before quoting it.

CML, TML, examination point, CML port: what the terms mean

Direct answer: a CML is a designated area on a piping circuit where periodic examinations are made to monitor its condition. TML (thickness measurement location) is the older term for the same idea when only thickness was monitored. An examination point is a spot inside a CML where a reading is taken. A "CML port" is usually an inspection plug or opening in insulation that gives access to a CML without stripping the insulation.

CML vs TML. API moved from TML to CML in the API 510 9th edition and API 570 3rd edition era. The change recognized that a monitoring location may track more than wall thickness. It might be a crack-susceptible weld, a CUI-prone area or a hot spot checked for creep or HTHA. Many plants still say "TML" for thickness points, and both terms appear in older data sets. When you merge inherited registers, map TML IDs to CML IDs one to one. Do not renumber them.

Examination point. A CML is an area, and an examination point is a location within it. Industry practice often treats a CML on pipe as a band or circle a few inches across, with one or more examination points. API 570 lets the inspector record either the thinnest reading or an average of several readings at an examination point. Choose one approach per CML and keep it. Switching between minimum and average from one campaign to the next produces corrosion rates that are artefacts.

Thickness monitoring location. This is a common plain-English name for a TML or thickness CML. Some owners also use "thickness monitoring point". The meaning is the same: a fixed, recorded spot where wall thickness is measured repeatedly so loss can be trended.

CML ports. On insulated lines, removing and replacing insulation at every CML each campaign is slow and expensive and can damage the jacketing. Owners therefore fit inspection ports: removable plugs or small openings in the insulation and jacketing at each CML, often with a cap or label. API 570 lists insulation plugs among the ways to identify examination points, along with stencils, isometrics, RFID tags and monitoring buttons. The risk is that a poorly sealed port lets water into the insulation and creates the CUI it was meant to help monitor. Ports need good caps, sealing and periodic checks. Spot readings through a small port can also miss localized attack beside it. That is why CUI programmes use ports alongside, not instead of, insulation removal at susceptible areas. See our page on corrosion under insulation inspection.

CML "in construction". In piping construction and commissioning, CML usually comes up as the baseline. API 570 says installation inspection should record baseline thickness readings at CMLs, to be used as the initial readings for corrosion rates instead of nominal thickness. A CML defined and measured at construction gives you the first point of every future trend. (In general construction, "CML" can also mean other things, such as a consolidated materials list. On a piping isometric it means a monitoring location.)

A step-by-step workflow for selecting CMLs

Direct answer: circuitize first, then assign damage mechanisms, then rate consequence and expected corrosion, then walk the isometric component by component placing CMLs where those mechanisms act. Size and mark the examination points, take baselines, and review the selection after the first two campaigns.

  1. Define the circuit. Group piping with the same material, process conditions and expected damage. Break the circuit at spec breaks, temperature changes, injection points and dead-leg boundaries.
  2. Assign credible damage mechanisms. Use API RP 571 and process knowledge: general thinning, localized corrosion, erosion-corrosion, under-deposit corrosion, CUI, high-temperature mechanisms, and cracking. API 570 says CML allocation should consider service-specific damage mechanisms, as described in API 574 and API 571. Our API 571 damage mechanisms guide is a starting point.
  3. Judge consequence and rate. Higher leak consequence, higher or more variable corrosion rates and higher localized-corrosion potential all call for more CMLs. Low consequence and low, stable rates allow fewer.
  4. Walk the isometric. Place CMLs at the components where the assigned mechanisms concentrate (see the placement table below). Add representative CMLs on straight runs so general thinning is also tracked.
  5. Decide coverage at each CML. How many examination points, which quadrants and which technique: spot, grid, scan, mapping or profile RT.
  6. Mark and identify. Number every CML uniquely on the inspection isometric and, where practical, on the pipe. Record orientation and offset from a permanent feature.
  7. Baseline. Measure every new CML before or soon after start-up. If the line is already in service, the first reading becomes the initial value for the long-term rate.
  8. Review. After two or more campaigns, compare rates across CMLs. Add CMLs where readings are scattered or rates are high. Consider reducing where history shows low, stable rates. Record the reasons.

The authorized piping inspector owns this process and consults a corrosion specialist where the code calls for one, for example before significantly reducing or eliminating CMLs.

Where CMLs go, component by component

Direct answer: fittings and flow disturbances get priority because turbulence and impingement concentrate damage. Dead legs, low points and soil-to-air interfaces get CMLs because water and deposits collect there. Spec breaks get CMLs on both sides. Straight runs get representative CMLs, more on longer or more corrosive runs.

Component or featureWhy it gets a CMLPlacement notes
Elbows and bendsErosion-corrosion and impingement on the outside radiusCover outside radius, inside radius and cheeks; four quadrants as appropriate
TeesFlow split and impingement at the branch and opposite wallRun and branch sides; area opposite the branch
Reducers and expandersVelocity change; turbulence downstreamOn the fitting and just downstream
Downstream of control valves and orificesTurbulence, flashing, cavitationSeveral diameters downstream, plus the first fitting
Dead legsStagnant fluid, water settling, depositsAt the low point and near the connection to the active line
Low points and drainsWater and solids collectBottom of line, at the 6 o'clock position
Injection and mix pointsLocalized attack from poorly mixed fluidOwn circuit; see our injection point guide
Soil-to-air interfacesMoisture and coating breakdown where pipe enters ground or concreteAt and just below the interface; may need excavation
Spec breaksMaterial change; different corrosion behaviourImmediately upstream and downstream
Insulated sections with CUI potentialWater under insulationAt penetrations, terminations, supports and low points
Long straight runsGeneral thinning trendRepresentative spacing; fewer on low-risk runs
Small-bore and threaded connectionsThin wall, vibration, threads remove metalFollow API 570's specific provisions; often covered by VT and RT

API 570 also lists conditions that justify more CMLs: higher leak consequence, higher or variable corrosion rates, localized-corrosion potential, complexity such as dead legs and injection points, CUI potential, process variability and industry failure history. Conditions for fewer CMLs include low consequence, relatively non-corrosive service and long straight runs. CMLs can be eliminated only in narrow cases, such as very low consequence with non-corrosive history and no expected change. Write down the reasoning whichever way you go.

Choosing the measurement technique at each CML

Direct answer: match the technique to the mechanism. Spot UT is fine for uniform thinning. Localized mechanisms need grid UT, scanning, PAUT corrosion mapping or profile radiography. A CML is only as good as its ability to find the minimum thickness in the area it represents.

Expected damageSuitable technique at the CMLNote
General uniform thinningSpot UT at fixed examination pointsKeep the same points and orientation each time
Erosion-corrosion at fittingsGrid UT or scanning over the fittingExtra attention to the elbow's outside radius
Pitting, under-deposit, MICPAUT corrosion mapping or close grid UTSpot readings commonly miss isolated pits
Bottom-of-line water attackCircumferential band scan or mappingFocus on 4 to 8 o'clock
Insulated linesProfile RT, or UT through ports after screeningProfile RT shows wall and deposits through insulation
Long runs, limited accessGuided-wave screening, then UT/RT at indicationsScreening locates; UT or RT sizes
Cracking mechanismsMT, PT, shear-wave UT, PAUT or TOFDChoose by mechanism and geometry

Thickness measurement should follow a written procedure with calibration on a reference block of the same material, temperature correction where the line is hot, and coating handling. Our article on UT thickness measurement requirements covers the details. For localized mechanisms, see corrosion mapping, and for profile work on insulated lines, radiographic testing.

Adding, moving and retiring CMLs without breaking the history

Direct answer: treat the CML register as a controlled record. Add CMLs when data or process changes justify it. Never move an existing CML silently; retire it and create a new one. Never reuse an ID. Record the reason for every change, especially reductions.

  • Adding. Add CMLs when readings at a location scatter widely, when the short-term rate jumps, when a new mechanism is found, or after a process change. A new CML starts its own history from its first reading.
  • Moving. If a CML was placed in the wrong spot, retire it and create a new one at the right place. Moving it under the same ID mixes two locations into one trend.
  • Retiring after replacement. When a spool or fitting is replaced, retire its CMLs and baseline new ones. The new metal has a new initial thickness.
  • Reducing. CML optimization is legitimate, but reductions should be reasoned, recorded and reviewed with a corrosion specialist where the code calls for it.
  • Management of change. Feedstock, temperature, velocity or chemical-treatment changes can bring new mechanisms. Link MOC to a CML review.

Our article on building a CML register that survives ten years covers ID rules and contractor handover in more depth.

A worked example, described qualitatively

Consider a carbon-steel naphtha line between two units. It runs about 200 feet, with eight elbows, two tees, a control valve, a dead-leg bypass and a section that goes underground at a road crossing. Part of it is insulated. The inspector sets it up like this:

  • Circuits. The main line is one circuit. The bypass dead leg is its own circuit because water can collect there. The road-crossing interface is flagged as a soil-to-air location.
  • Mechanisms. General thinning and erosion-corrosion at fittings, under-deposit corrosion in the dead leg, CUI on the insulated section and external corrosion at the soil-to-air interface.
  • CMLs. One on each elbow and tee, one downstream of the control valve, representative CMLs on the straight runs, two in the dead leg (low point and junction), CMLs at insulation terminations and supports, and CMLs at both sides of the soil-to-air interface.
  • Techniques. Grid UT on fittings, mapping in the dead leg, profile RT on the insulated section with ports at selected CMLs, and VT plus UT at the interface after excavation.
  • Review. After the second campaign, two elbows show higher rates. The inspector adds a CML on the next elbow downstream and changes those CMLs from grid to mapping. Straight-run CMLs with stable, low rates are kept but not increased.

The point is that every CML has a reason tied to a mechanism, a technique matched to that mechanism, and a record of why it exists.

Common CML selection mistakes, and the jurisdiction note

Direct answer: the usual mistakes are placing CMLs where access is easy rather than where damage happens, spacing them evenly by length, using spot readings for localized mechanisms, and changing CMLs without records. All of them weaken the corrosion rates the inspection interval depends on.

  • CMLs placed on easy-to-reach straight runs while fittings are skipped.
  • Even spacing by length, with no link to mechanism.
  • No CMLs in dead legs, at low points or at soil-to-air interfaces.
  • Insulation ports left unsealed, creating CUI.
  • Single spot readings where pitting is the expected mechanism.
  • CML IDs reused or renumbered when isometrics are redrawn.
  • Nominal thickness used as the initial reading because no baseline was taken.

In the United States, OSHA PSM (29 CFR 1910.119(j)) requires inspection and testing following recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and API 570 with API RP 574 is the common reference for process piping. In Canada, provincial regulators such as ABSA in Alberta and TSSA in Ontario oversee pressure piping, with CSA B51 as the base code and owner-user programme requirements in some provinces. Confirm the rules that apply with your jurisdiction.

More CML questions

What are CML ports?

Inspection plugs or openings in pipe insulation at condition monitoring locations. They let technicians take UT readings without stripping insulation. They must be well sealed, because a leaking port lets water in and causes corrosion under insulation.

What is a thickness monitoring location?

A fixed, recorded spot on a pipe where wall thickness is measured repeatedly to trend corrosion. API 570 called it a TML in older editions and now uses the broader term condition monitoring location (CML).

What are condition monitoring locations (CMLs)?

Designated areas on piping or equipment where periodic examinations monitor condition. That usually means thickness, but it can include other damage such as cracking or CUI. Each CML has a unique ID, a marked position and a reading history.

What does CML mean in inspection?

Condition monitoring location. It is the basic unit of a piping inspection plan: readings at the same CML over time give the corrosion rate, remaining life and next inspection date.

What does CML mean in construction?

On piping construction, CML refers to the monitoring locations defined on isometrics and baselined at installation. Those first readings become the initial thickness for future corrosion rates instead of nominal thickness.

Is a TML the same as a CML?

Essentially yes for thickness. TML is the older term; CML is broader and can include monitoring for other damage mechanisms.

Who selects CMLs on a piping circuit?

The owner's API 570 authorized piping inspector, with a corrosion specialist where needed. NDE contractors measure at the CMLs and can flag locations that look under-covered.
